title: UK Driving Theory Test (Car)
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public DVSA theory test syllabus. Not a copy of the official question bank.

items.stem: You are three hours into a long motorway journey and your concentration is beginning to drift. What is the safest way to deal with this?
options: Leave at the next exit, stop somewhere safe and take a break of at least 15 minutes
Turn the radio up and open a window to stay awake for the rest of the journey
Drive faster so that the journey is finished more quickly
Ask a passenger to talk to you and carry on driving without stopping
items.explanation: A break of at least 15 minutes every two hours is the recommended remedy for fading concentration. Opening a window or turning up the radio only masks tiredness briefly, and pressing on raises crash risk.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are stopped in a long queue of traffic at red lights and your mobile phone rings. What is the rule about answering it on a handheld handset?
options: Handheld use is fine as long as the vehicle is not moving
Using a handheld phone while driving is illegal, including when stopped in traffic
It is legal if the call lasts less than a minute and you keep watching the road
It is legal when you are stationary on a flat road but not when on a hill
items.explanation: The law treats you as driving whenever the engine is running in traffic, so handheld use is an offence carrying six points and a fine. Only hands-free use that does not distract you is permitted.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are driving along a quiet residential road at a steady speed. How often should you check your mirrors so that you stay aware of what is happening around you?
options: Only when you are about to turn or change direction
Only when a vehicle sounds its horn behind you
About every five to eight seconds, as a routine
Only when you can hear traffic approaching from behind
items.explanation: Regular mirror checks roughly every five to eight seconds keep you informed of traffic building up behind and of vehicles entering your blind spots, rather than only reacting when a manoeuvre is planned.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You begin to nod off as you drive along a long, straight dual carriageway. What should you do?
options: Increase your speed to shorten the journey
Turn the air conditioning up full and carry on driving
Move to the outside lane so that other drivers can get past you
Leave at the next exit, find a safe place to park and rest
items.explanation: Once drowsiness sets in, only sleep restores alertness, so the safe response is to stop in a legal, safe place and rest. Air conditioning and speed changes disguise the problem without solving it.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are driving through a built-up area with the car stereo playing loudly. Why can this make your driving less safe?
options: It can mask the sound of sirens, horns and developing hazards
It uses extra battery power that could flatten the alternator
It is an offence to listen to any music while driving a car
It causes the tyres to warm up more quickly than normal
items.explanation: Hearing helps you pick up approaching emergency vehicles, horns and unusual engine or tyre noises, so loud music that drowns those cues removes an early warning you would otherwise act on.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: A driver is following you far too closely on a wet road. What is the safest response?
options: Brake sharply now and then to warn them to back off
Ease off gradually, increase the gap ahead and let them pass when it is safe
Speed up until the driver falls behind you
Steer from side to side across the lane to block them
items.explanation: Braking hard or swerving only raises the risk of a collision, while increasing your own gap gives both drivers more stopping room and letting the tailgater past removes the hazard without confrontation.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You have been prescribed an antihistamine that may cause drowsiness. What should you check before driving?
options: Whether the tablets have passed their expiry date
Whether you can take a double dose so that you stay alert
Whether the medicine warns against driving, by asking your pharmacist or doctor
Whether you have eaten a large meal before taking them
items.explanation: Many medicines carry warnings about drowsiness and driving, and a pharmacist or doctor can confirm whether it is safe for you. Expiry dates, dose increases and full stomachs do not answer that question.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You need to program a route into your satellite navigation system. When is the correct time to do this?
options: At the next set of red lights while the vehicle is stopped
From the driver's seat between junctions while moving
While a passenger watches the road and you press the buttons
Before you start the journey, while the vehicle is parked
items.explanation: Anything that takes attention from the road is a distraction, so routes should be set before moving off. Even entering a destination at red lights cuts the time available to spot developing hazards.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You flash your headlights at a car waiting to emerge from a side road. What have you actually told that driver?
options: You are letting them know that you are there
They have priority and should go first
They may pull out ahead of you with confidence
You are about to stop and give them way
items.explanation: The only official meaning of a headlight flash is to warn others of your presence, so the other driver must not treat it as an invitation. If you intend to give way, slow clearly and stop instead.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are driving at 30 mph and are about to pass a cyclist riding in the road. What clearance should you leave?
options: As little as half a metre if you creep past slowly
At least 1.5 metres, and more if you are travelling faster
Exactly the width of your door mirror
One metre, but only if there is no traffic coming the other way
items.explanation: The Highway Code asks for at least 1.5 metres when passing riders at up to 30 mph and a wider gap above that speed, because buffeting or a sudden swerve can easily knock a cyclist off.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are approaching a sharp bend with a solid white line down the middle and no view of the road ahead. What should you do?
options: Move towards the centre of the road so you can see further round it
Accelerate so that you spend less time on the bend
Slow down before the bend and stay on your own side of the line
Sound your horn continuously while you go round
items.explanation: Speed should be scrubbed off before a bend you cannot see round so the car stays controllable and can stop within the road you can actually see. Crossing the centre line invites a head-on collision.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: A pedestrian steps towards a zebra crossing while looking down at a phone. What is the safest assumption for you to make?
options: They have seen you and will wait for you to pass
They will cross behind your vehicle rather than in front
The crossing rules do not apply until they step onto it
They have not seen you, so be ready to stop
items.explanation: Pedestrians waiting to cross have priority at a zebra crossing, and someone absorbed in a phone is unlikely to have registered your approach, so you should slow and stop rather than assume you are noticed.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are driving slowly past an ice cream van with several children standing beside it. What should you expect?
options: Children may run out suddenly, so reduce speed and be ready to stop
Children will wait for the van to move off before crossing
The van will stay stationary until you have passed it
Children are not permitted near any vehicle on the road
items.explanation: Children focus on the van rather than on traffic and can dart between parked cars without looking, so a low speed and a foot covering the brake give you the stopping distance you may suddenly need.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are about to move off from the kerb after picking up a passenger. Why is a shoulder check still necessary when you have already used your mirrors?
options: A shoulder check is only required before joining a motorway
Mirrors do not show vehicles or cyclists alongside or just behind your blind spots
Mirrors only show what is directly in front of the car
A shoulder check replaces the need to signal before moving
items.explanation: Door mirrors leave gaps immediately beside and just behind the car where a motorcycle or cyclist can sit, so a look over the shoulder closes that gap before you alter your position.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are driving towards the crest of a hill on a narrow country road. How should you approach it?
options: Keep your speed up so that you clear the crest quickly
Move on to the wrong side of the road to see over the top
Slow down before the crest because you cannot see what is beyond
Flash your headlights to warn any oncoming traffic
items.explanation: Nothing beyond a crest is visible and an oncoming vehicle may be close to the top, so an approach speed that lets you stop within the visible part of the road is the only safe choice.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Alertness and Safety

items.stem: You are checking the tyres on your car before a long journey. What is the legal minimum tread depth for a car?
options: 1.0 mm across the whole of the tread
1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the tread and around the whole circumference
2.0 mm on the outer edges only
3.0 mm across the entire tyre
items.explanation: Cars must have at least 1.6 mm of tread in the central three-quarters of the tyre and around its entire circumference. Below that, wet grip falls sharply and the tyre fails its MOT test.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: You notice that one tyre on your car is noticeably softer than the others. What effect can driving on it have?
options: The tyre will wear away in the centre of the tread
The steering will feel unusually light at high speed
The tyre can overheat, wear on the outer edges and make steering heavier
Fuel consumption will fall because rolling resistance drops
items.explanation: An under-inflated tyre flexes excessively, which builds heat, wears the outer edges and raises fuel use while making the steering feel heavy. It also increases the risk of a blow-out.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: It has been raining steadily and the road surface is wet. How should you adjust the gap to the vehicle in front?
options: No change is needed if you are driving below 30 mph
Leave the same gap as in dry conditions but start braking earlier
Leave about half the dry-conditions gap because water cools the brakes
At least double the stopping distance you would need in dry conditions
items.explanation: Wet roads at least double stopping distances because tyres cannot clear water as quickly, so twice the dry gap is the minimum. On ice the gap may need to be as much as ten times greater.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: You are loading heavy boxes into the boot of a small car for a motorway journey. How should the weight be placed?
options: Low down, evenly spread and as close to the centre of the car as possible
On the back seat so that the boot door closes properly
Stacked as high as possible so that nothing can slide out
Hard against the rear door so the weight sits at the very back
items.explanation: Keeping weight low, central and evenly spread stops the car becoming top-heavy or tail-heavy, which would upset its balance under braking and make the steering vague at motorway speeds.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: You fit a loaded roof box to your car for a holiday journey. Which statement about it is correct?
options: Fuel consumption falls because the car is lighter at the front
It increases air resistance and fuel use, and raises the overall height of the vehicle
It has no effect on handling provided the roof rails are tight
It improves stability in cross-winds
items.explanation: A roof box disrupts airflow, so it increases fuel consumption and makes the car more affected by side winds. The extra height must also be allowed for at height barriers and low bridges.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: Your car has anti-lock brakes and you must brake hard to avoid a child stepping into the road. What should you do?
options: Pump the brake pedal rapidly to stop the wheels locking
Release the brake pedal completely as soon as the wheels lock
Keep firm steady pressure on the pedal and steer around the obstacle
Pull the handbrake on to help slow the car
items.explanation: Anti-lock brakes are fitted so that steering stays available under heavy braking, so you should hold firm pressure and steer. Pumping the pedal or snatching the handbrake defeats the system.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: The rear of your car begins to slide out on a wet road. What is the best first action?
options: Apply the footbrake hard to slow the car at once
Turn the steering wheel sharply the opposite way to the slide
Press the clutch down and coast until control returns
Ease off the accelerator and steer gently in the direction of the skid
items.explanation: Skids are usually caused by speed that is too high for the conditions, so easing off the accelerator reduces the demand on the tyres while gentle steering in the direction of the skid brings the rear back in line.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: You are towing a caravan with your car on a dual carriageway in clear conditions. What is the maximum speed limit for your combination?
options: 50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
40 mph
items.explanation: A car towing a caravan or trailer is limited to 50 mph on single and dual carriageways and 60 mph on motorways, whatever the road's normal limit is. The full 70 mph applies only to cars towing nothing.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: Thick fog has reduced your visibility to about 60 metres. When may you use your rear fog light?
options: Only on an unlit motorway
Whenever visibility falls below 100 metres, switching it off when the fog clears
Throughout a foggy night even when you can see clearly
Only when your vehicle is stationary
items.explanation: Rear fog lights may be used when visibility drops below 100 metres so that following drivers see you sooner, but they must be switched off when it improves because they dazzle the driver behind.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: You park on the right-hand side of a road facing downhill with a kerb beside the car. Where should the front wheels point?
options: Straight ahead so the car is easy to drive away
Away from the kerb so that the car rolls clear of it
Towards the kerb so the car rests against it if the brakes fail
Towards the centre of the road so the car rolls off the roadway
items.explanation: Turning the wheels towards the kerb when facing downhill means the car rolls into the kerb rather than into the road if the brakes release, which is the standard precaution when parking on a slope.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: You are driving at night on an unlit country road with no other traffic around you. What should you do with your headlights?
options: Use dipped headlights only, so you never dazzle yourself
Switch the headlights off to save the battery
Use side lights only until you meet another vehicle
Use main beam to see as far ahead as possible, dipping for approaching traffic
items.explanation: Main beam gives the longest view on an unlit road when nothing is close enough to be dazzled, and you dip to headlights when you meet or follow other traffic or enter a lit area.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: The temperature gauge on your dashboard moves into the red while you are driving. What should you do?
options: Stop as soon as it is safe, switch off the engine and let it cool before investigating
Keep driving to your destination and top up the coolant when you arrive
Drive faster so that more air passes through the radiator
Turn the heater up to maximum and ignore the gauge
items.explanation: An overheating engine can be badly damaged within minutes, so pull over and let it cool. Opening the filler cap of a hot radiator straight away can also release steam that causes serious scalding.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: How often should you check the tyre pressures on your car?
options: Only when a tyre visibly looks flat
At least once a fortnight and before a long or heavily loaded journey
Once a year, just before the MOT test
Only after driving at high speed on a motorway
items.explanation: Tyres lose pressure gradually without looking flat, so fortnightly checks when the tyres are cold, plus checks before long journeys, keep grip, fuel use and steering response at their best.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: The brake pedal on your car feels spongy and sinks almost to the floor. What does this suggest?
options: The tyres need more air
The engine is running too rich
There is air or lost fluid in the braking system, so the car should not be driven
The car needs a four-wheel alignment
items.explanation: A spongy pedal usually points to air in the hydraulic circuit or leaking brake fluid, both of which can end in brake failure, so the vehicle should be recovered and repaired rather than driven.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: The red battery warning light stays on after you start your car and is still lit as you drive off. What does it indicate?
options: The tyres are under-inflated
The engine needs new spark plugs
The fuel tank is nearly empty
The charging system is not working and the battery is running down
items.explanation: That light normally means the alternator has stopped charging the battery, so switch off non-essential electrical items and stop safely before the engine cuts out and leaves you stranded.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Vehicle Safety and Handling

items.stem: The traffic lights at the junction ahead show red and amber together. What should you do?
options: Move off at once because amber means get ready to go
Move off slowly if the road ahead looks clear
Stop at the line and wait for a green light alone
Sound your horn and edge forward to the line
items.explanation: Red and amber shown together still means stop. You wait behind the line until green appears on its own, and only continue if the lights changed when you had already crossed the line.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are waiting at a set of traffic lights and a green filter arrow appears pointing left. What does this allow you to do?
options: Turn left without looking at other traffic at all
Overtake any vehicle ahead of you in the queue
Go in any direction you wish while the arrow shows
Turn left only if the way is clear and you give way to anyone still in the junction
items.explanation: A filter arrow only protects you from traffic that the main signals are holding back, so you must still check the left turn is clear and let vehicles already in the junction finish before you move.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are looking for a place to park near a zebra crossing and you notice zigzag white lines painted on the road. What do they mean?
options: Waiting and parking are not allowed on or across the zigzags
You may park there briefly as long as you stay in the car
Parking is permitted there for residents only
Overtaking is allowed but parking is not
items.explanation: The zigzag lines keep the approaches to the crossing clear so pedestrians and drivers can see each other, so no waiting or parking is allowed on them and overtaking the leading vehicle is also prohibited.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You see a circular blue sign showing a single white arrow pointing upwards. What is the meaning of this sign?
options: One-way road ahead
Ahead only
You may turn left or right at the junction
No motor vehicles beyond this point
items.explanation: A blue circle with one upward arrow is a mandatory sign telling you to proceed straight ahead only. A one-way street is shown instead by a rectangular blue sign with a white arrow.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are approaching a roundabout and intend to take the third exit to the right. Which lane and signal should you use on the approach?
options: Left lane, with no signal until you have passed the second exit
Left lane, with a signal to the left on the approach
Right lane, with a signal to the right on the approach
Either lane, as long as you signal once you are on the roundabout
items.explanation: Turning right means using the right-hand lane and signalling right on approach, then signalling left after you pass the exit before yours. Taking the left lane for a right turn cuts across other traffic.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are driving on a road with double white lines where the line nearest to you is solid. When may you cross them?
options: Whenever you wish to overtake a slow-moving vehicle
Only during hours of darkness
Whenever the road ahead is clear of oncoming traffic
Only for specific reasons such as entering premises or passing a stationary vehicle
items.explanation: A solid line on your side means you must not cross or straddle the lines except in narrow cases such as turning into a property or passing a stationary vehicle. A broken line on your side would allow crossing when safe.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are driving along a red route and see double red lines painted beside the kerb. What do they mean?
options: No stopping at any time
No waiting, but passengers may still be set down
Parking allowed for up to fifteen minutes
No loading except at weekends
items.explanation: Double red lines mean stopping is prohibited at any time, with exemptions only for emergency and certain service vehicles. Single red lines already forbid waiting but are less restrictive than a double pair.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You approach a junction controlled by a sign shaped like an upside-down triangle with a red border. What does it require of you?
options: Stop completely, even if the road is clear
Give way to traffic on the road you are joining
Proceed ahead of the traffic on the major road
Carry on at a reduced speed without stopping
items.explanation: The inverted triangle is the give-way sign, so you must slow and be ready to stop for traffic on the major road. The octagonal stop sign is the one that forces a full halt whatever the view.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are driving a car on a single carriageway road where a white circle with a black diagonal stripe applies. What is the maximum speed in good conditions?
options: 30 mph
50 mph
60 mph
70 mph
items.explanation: The national speed limit sign means 60 mph for a car on a single carriageway and 70 mph on a dual carriageway or motorway, with lower limits for vehicles such as vans and cars towing trailers.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are joining a motorway from a slip road and traffic is already using the carriageway. What should you do?
options: Stop at the end of the slip road until a gap appears
Flash your headlights so that traffic moves over for you
Join at a much slower speed and force a gap in the traffic
Adjust your speed to fit into a gap and give way to traffic already on the motorway
items.explanation: Traffic already on the motorway has priority, so use the slip road to match its speed and merge smoothly. Stopping or crawling at the end blocks the slip road and endangers the vehicles behind you.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are driving along a quiet three-lane motorway and the left-hand lane is empty ahead of you. Where should you be driving?
options: In the left-hand lane
In the centre lane so you can move either way
In the right-hand lane so you are ready to overtake
In whichever lane you prefer, provided you keep to the limit
items.explanation: The left lane is the normal driving lane and the others are for overtaking only, so returning to it after passing keeps traffic moving and avoids the queueing caused by cruising in the middle lane.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are approaching a crossroads that has no road markings and no signs. Who has priority there?
options: Traffic arriving from the right, always
No one has priority, so approach ready to stop
Traffic going straight ahead over traffic turning
Whichever vehicle is the largest
items.explanation: Priorities at an unmarked crossroads are not defined, so drivers must negotiate carefully and be ready to give way. Assuming you have priority is a common cause of collisions when turning right.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You reach a junction with a red octagonal sign reading STOP and the road ahead looks completely clear. What must you do?
options: Slow to walking pace and continue if nothing is coming
Stop only if another vehicle is visible
Come to a complete stop at the line every time
Sound your horn and proceed without stopping
items.explanation: The octagonal stop sign is the only sign that always requires a full stop at the line, whatever the view appears to show, before you move off again when it is safe to do so.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are driving behind a bus that is signalling and moving out from a bus stop. What should you do?
options: Overtake quickly before it reaches the traffic queue
Sound your horn to tell the driver that you are there
Stay level with the bus so that it cannot move out
Give way if it is safe to do so and let the bus pull out
items.explanation: A bus full of passengers has a good reason to rejoin the traffic flow and should be given way to when signalling to move off, so hold back where possible and only pass if you can do so safely.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: At a pelican crossing the amber light is flashing and the pedestrians have nearly finished crossing. What may you do?
options: Move off if the crossing is clear and you can do so safely
Move off immediately, because flashing amber means go
Sound your horn to hurry the remaining pedestrians along
Remain stopped until a steady green light shows again
items.explanation: Flashing amber at a pelican crossing tells pedestrians to finish crossing and lets drivers go when the way is clear. It is not an instruction to move regardless of people still on the crossing.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Road Procedures and Signs

items.stem: You are the first person on the scene of a collision in which a car has left the road and its driver is injured. What should you do first?
options: Move the injured driver to a place of safety
Ask a bystander to take photographs before anything else
Give the injured driver a drink to help them recover
Warn other traffic, stop the engine if safe and call the emergency services
items.explanation: Protecting the scene prevents further collisions and a 999 call brings professional help. Moving a casualty unnecessarily can worsen spinal injuries, and drinks are unsafe if surgery may follow.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: A motorcyclist is lying injured at the roadside after a collision. What is the correct action regarding their helmet?
options: Leave it on unless it is essential to remove it to keep the airway clear
Remove it immediately so that they can breathe more easily
Remove it so that you can check the head for injuries
Take it off to make the casualty more comfortable
items.explanation: The helmet supports the head and neck, so it stays in place. It is removed only when absolutely necessary, for example to clear an obstructed airway or when the casualty has stopped breathing.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: A casualty has a deep cut to the arm and blood is pumping out of it. What should you do?
options: Apply a tourniquet at once and leave it in place
Press firmly on the wound with a clean pad and raise the arm above heart level
Give the casualty food and drink while you wait for help
Wash the wound thoroughly with cold water before anything else
items.explanation: Firm direct pressure slows bleeding fastest and raising the limb above the heart helps further. A tourniquet is a last resort and washing the wound first wastes time while blood is being lost.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: A passenger burns their hand on a hot exhaust pipe at the roadside. What is the best immediate treatment?
options: Spread butter or cream over the burn
Cover the burn with a dry dressing straight away
Cool the burn under cool running water for at least 20 minutes
Break any blisters so that the heat can escape
items.explanation: Cool running water stops a burn going deeper and relieves pain, ideally for 20 minutes. Butter, creams and bursting blisters all raise the risk of infection and further tissue damage.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: You are involved in a collision that damages another vehicle but injures no one, and the other driver leaves before giving details. What must you do?
options: Nothing at all, because nobody was hurt
Write to your insurer within a month
Report the matter to the DVLA the following week
Report the collision to the police as soon as possible and in any case within 24 hours
items.explanation: You must stop and, if you cannot exchange details, report the collision to the police at the earliest opportunity and within 24 hours. Failing to do so is an offence under the road traffic legislation.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: What is the minimum level of motor insurance you must carry to drive legally on a public road?
options: Third party only
Third party, fire and theft
Comprehensive cover
No insurance at all for short journeys
items.explanation: Third party is the legal minimum because it covers injury to other people and damage to their property. Fire and theft, and comprehensive cover, add protection for your own vehicle on top of that.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: From what age does a car in the UK normally need its first MOT test?
options: One year old
Three years old
Five years old
Seven years old
items.explanation: Cars must be tested from the third anniversary of their first registration and then every 12 months. Driving without a valid MOT when one is required brings a fine and usually invalidates insurance.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: You have sold your car privately to a buyer. What must you do to keep the registration records correct?
options: Keep the V5C registration certificate in case of a claim
Do nothing, because the buyer will inform the DVLA
Send the relevant part of the V5C to the DVLA or notify them online straight away
Hand over the keys and wait for the DVLA to write to you
items.explanation: The seller must notify DVLA of the change of keeper by returning the V5C or using the online service. Until that is done you remain linked to the vehicle and to any offences committed with it.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: Your car is beyond economic repair and you want to scrap it. What is the correct procedure?
options: Leave it on a private garage forecourt and walk away
Sell it to any passer-by for spare parts
Remove the wheels and take the rest to the local tip
Take it to an authorised treatment facility and obtain a Certificate of Destruction
items.explanation: Only an authorised treatment facility may scrap a vehicle, and it must issue a Certificate of Destruction. You should also send the relevant documentation to DVLA so that your responsibility ends.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: Your car breaks down on a straight rural road that is not a motorway. Where should you place the warning triangle?
options: At least 45 metres behind the vehicle
Directly in front of the vehicle
Beside the driver's door
On the roof of the vehicle
items.explanation: A triangle placed at least 45 metres behind a stopped vehicle on a straight road gives approaching drivers early warning. It must never be used on a motorway hard shoulder, where it would put you at risk.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: Your car breaks down on the hard shoulder of a motorway at night. Where should you and your passengers wait?
options: Inside the car with seatbelts fastened and the engine running
Outside the vehicle and behind the safety barrier, away from the carriageway
On the hard shoulder in front of the car so that you are visible
In the right-hand lane to warn other drivers
items.explanation: Standing behind the barrier puts a crush zone between you and moving traffic. If you must stay with the car, everyone should leave by the left-hand side and wear high-visibility clothing.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: What is the maximum legal alcohol limit in breath for a driver in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
options: 50 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath
80 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath
35 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath
20 micrograms of alcohol per 100 millilitres of breath
items.explanation: The breath limit is 35 micrograms per 100 millilitres, which corresponds to 80 milligrams per 100 millilitres of blood and 67 milligrams per 100 millilitres of urine. Even small amounts impair driving.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: You are caught exceeding the speed limit and are offered a fixed penalty by the camera operator's scheme. What is the usual penalty?
options: A written warning with no penalty
Two penalty points and a £100 fine
A compulsory retake of the theory test
Three penalty points and a £100 fixed penalty fine
items.explanation: Speeding normally brings a fixed penalty of three points and £100. A court can impose up to six points plus a larger fine, and some police forces offer a speed awareness course instead where eligible.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: What eyesight standard must you meet before you are allowed to take the practical driving test?
options: Read a modern number plate in good daylight at 20 metres
Have perfect colour vision in both eyes
Have 6/6 vision in both eyes without wearing glasses
Read a number plate in good daylight at 40 metres
items.explanation: You must read, in good daylight, a modern number plate at 20 metres, which is 20.5 metres for the newer style, and meet the minimum field of vision. Glasses or lenses may be worn to do this.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation

items.stem: A police officer stops you and finds that you are driving a car without insurance. What could happen?
options: You will simply be asked to buy cover at the roadside
You can be given six penalty points and a £300 fixed penalty, or be taken to court
Nothing, as long as you hold a valid MOT certificate for the car
Your licence is endorsed with a free caution and no points
items.explanation: Driving uninsured can bring six penalty points and a fixed penalty of up to £300, or court proceedings leading to an unlimited fine and disqualification. The vehicle may also be seized at the roadside.
items.reference: DVSA Theory Test Syllabus - Incidents and Documentation
